title: Web Accessibility Practice
description: Practise the twelve ideas in this Web Accessibility course. Choose an answer, then read why it fits the example.

exercises.question: Which element already supports button keyboard behaviour?
options: button
div
exercises.explanation: A button already knows how to work with a keyboard. A plain div does not become a button just because it looks like one.

exercises.question: Why use headings in a sensible order?
options: They automatically translate all words
They describe the page structure
exercises.explanation: Headings tell readers how a page is organised. A screen reader can list headings to help someone move between topics.

exercises.question: Which element identifies the main content?
options: main
span
exercises.explanation: Elements such as nav and main name big page regions. These names help reading tools offer shortcuts.

exercises.question: Why does the decorative flower use alt=""?
options: It tells the browser to read its file name
It adds no information that needs to be read
exercises.explanation: Alternative text describes a useful image for someone who cannot see it. Decorative images use an empty alt value.

exercises.question: Which two values need to match?
options: The label for and input id
The label words and the CSS colour
exercises.explanation: A visible label explains what to type. Matching its for value with an input id links the two parts.

exercises.question: What belongs in aria-describedby?
options: A random colour name
The id of the help element
exercises.explanation: A field can have a short help message as well as a label. aria-describedby connects the field to that extra explanation.

exercises.question: Why is a focus outline useful?
options: It shows where keyboard actions will go
It hides controls from screen readers
exercises.explanation: Focus is the place that will receive the next key action. A visible outline shows that place to someone using a keyboard.

exercises.question: What problem does a skip link help solve?
options: Storing passwords in a browser
Passing the same navigation on every page
exercises.explanation: A skip link lets a keyboard user move past repeated navigation and straight to the main content.

exercises.question: Which link wording is more useful on its own?
options: Read the garden club timetable
Click here
exercises.explanation: Link words should make sense when read on their own. Clear words tell a reader where a link will go.

exercises.question: Does a status message need to steal focus?
options: Yes, every update must move focus
No, it can be announced without moving focus
exercises.explanation: A polite live region can announce a small update without moving keyboard focus. It is useful for a saved message or a count.

exercises.question: What does prefers-reduced-motion check?
options: The person's motion preference
The number of pictures on a page
exercises.explanation: Some people feel unwell when a page moves a lot. The reduced-motion setting asks pages to use less movement.

exercises.question: Can one automated check prove a page has no accessibility problems?
options: Yes, it proves every task works
No, manual checks are needed too
exercises.explanation: Accessibility testing needs more than one check. Keyboard use, zoom, contrast tools and screen readers each reveal different problems.
